intro: Put a drop of pond water under a microscope and a hidden world appears: cells spinning, darting, and splitting in two. Look at a slice of onion skin and you see a neat grid of boxes, each with a dark dot at its center. Every living thing you have ever seen, from a bacterium to a blue whale, is built from cells like these. You are made of roughly 30 trillion of them, and every one started from a single cell.

This unit follows life from that tiny scale up to whole bodies and whole behaviors. You will learn what a cell is and what its parts do, how cells stack into tissues, organs, and systems, and how those systems keep you alive together. You will trace where the energy in a sandwich or a sunbeam goes, how a nerve carries a signal from your toe to your brain, and how a bee remembers a patch of clover.

Then you will look at the ways living things make sure there is a next generation: fireflies flashing codes, flowers paying bees in sugar, maple seeds spinning away on the wind, and penguins guarding a single egg through the winter. By the end you should be able to explain how matter and energy flow through living things, how organisms sense and respond to their world, and why growth depends on both the genes an organism inherits and the environment it grows up in.
bigQuestion: How do cells, bodies, and behaviors work together to keep living things alive and make the next generation?

timeline.t: William Harvey argues from measurements that blood circulates around the body
Van Helmont's willow experiment is published: a tree gains 164 pounds while the soil loses 2 ounces
Robert Hooke looks at cork through a microscope and names the little boxes cells
Leeuwenhoek reports tiny living animalcules swimming in a drop of pepper water
Joseph Priestley finds that a sprig of mint restores used-up air so a candle can burn again
Jan Ingenhousz shows plants give off oxygen only from green parts and only in light
Schleiden and Schwann argue that all plants and all animals are made of cells
Rudolf Virchow states that every cell comes from a cell
Ivan Pavlov wins a Nobel Prize for his work on digestion, alongside his studies of learned reflexes in dogs
Golgi and Cajal share a Nobel Prize for revealing the structure of the nervous system
The electron microscope is built, showing the insides of cells in fine detail

words.d: the smallest unit of a living thing that is itself alive
the organelle that holds a cell's DNA instructions
organelles that break down food with oxygen to release energy for the cell
a green organelle in plant cells that captures light energy to make sugar
a group of similar cells that work together on one job
a group of organs that work together toward one goal, such as moving blood
the process in which plants use light to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen
the process in which cells break sugar down with oxygen to release energy
a cell that turns light, sound, heat, pressure, or a chemical into a nerve signal
a nerve cell that carries electrical signals through the body
an animal that carries pollen from one flower to another
an experiment in which only one factor is changed and everything else is kept the same

test.q: Which of these is a living thing made of a single cell?
test.why: Bacteria are unicellular. A leaf and a mosquito are made of many cells, and salt is not alive.

test.q: Which structure do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
test.why: Plant cells have a stiff cell wall and chloroplasts. Both kinds of cell have a nucleus, a membrane, and mitochondria.

choices: A single cell with a big job
A body part made of several tissues that does a specific job
test.why: The heart, for example, is made of muscle, nerve, and connective tissue working together.

test.q: Oxygen enters your blood in the lungs. Which system then carries it to your muscles?
test.why: The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood through vessels to every cell.

test.q: Why do muscles come in pairs, such as the biceps and triceps?
choices: A muscle can only pull, so a partner must pull the other way
Bones need two muscles to stay strong
Nerves can only reach two muscles at a time
test.why: Muscles shorten but cannot push. One bends the joint and its partner straightens it.

test.q: A reflex pulls your hand from a hot pan before you feel pain. Why?
choices: The brain is faster than the spinal cord
The spinal cord sends the response before the signal reaches the brain
Muscles can feel heat on their own
test.why: Reflexes are handled in the spinal cord for speed; the feeling arrives when the signal reaches the brain.

test.q: Which of these is a product of photosynthesis?
test.why: Plants use light, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar and release oxygen.

test.q: Which organisms carry out cellular respiration?
choices: Plants, animals, and other living things all do
test.why: Every living cell must release energy from food, so every organism respires.

test.q: Van Helmont's willow gained about 164 pounds in five years. Where did most of that mass come from?
choices: Water and carbon dioxide from the air
test.why: The soil lost only about 2 ounces. The mass came from water and, as later shown, carbon dioxide.

test.q: A bee can see ultraviolet patterns on a flower that you cannot. What is the reason?
choices: Bees are closer to the flower
Bees have receptors for ultraviolet light and humans do not
test.why: Which light a creature can see depends on the receptors in its eyes.

test.q: In Pavlov's experiment, dogs drooled at a ticking sound with no food present. What does this show?
choices: Sounds cause hunger in all animals
Experiences that happen together become linked in the brain
Dogs are born knowing metronomes mean food
test.why: Repeated pairing of sound and food created a learned connection, a memory that changed behavior.

test.q: Why does a male firefly flash a specific pattern?
choices: To attract a female of its own species
test.why: Flash patterns are courtship signals, and each species has its own so mates can find each other.

test.q: Which is an example of seed dispersal by wind?
choices: A dandelion seed drifting on a fluffy tuft
A burr stuck to a dog's fur
A coconut floating on the sea
test.why: Parachutes and wings catch the wind. The others use animals or water.

test.q: A salmon lays thousands of eggs and gives no care. An emperor penguin lays one egg and guards it for months. What is true?
choices: Both are strategies that can keep a species going
test.why: Many-and-cheap and few-and-costly are both ways to have enough offspring survive.

test.q: Two bean plants from the same packet grow to different heights. What is the best explanation?
choices: Height is not affected by anything
test.why: Seeds from one packet share nearly the same genes, so conditions like light and water explain the difference.

write.prompt: Make a claim: the material in a growing plant comes mostly from the air and water, not from the soil. Support it with evidence from van Helmont's willow, Priestley's mint, Ingenhousz's bubbles, and what you know about photosynthesis, and explain how the evidence supports the claim.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Use numbers as evidence: the willow gained about 164 pounds while the soil lost about 2 ounces.
Explain the reasoning: what does photosynthesis take in, and where does the carbon in wood come from?
Address the other side: why do people assume plants are made of soil, and what does the soil actually provide?
End by saying what new evidence could change your mind.
